n: Isaiah 10 begins with woe to lawmakers who write unjust laws and oppressive decrees.
Their laws deny justice to the needy, steal the rights of the poor, and prey on widows and orphans — the very people God commands His people to protect.

f.w: that widows may be their prey

n: What will they do on the day of reckoning when disaster comes from afar? Where will they run, and where will they leave their wealth?
They will cower among the prisoners or fall among the dead. The refrain sounds a last time: His hand is still stretched out.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

n: God addresses Assyria as the rod of His anger — the tool He uses to discipline His people.

f.w: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger

n: God sends Assyria against godless Judah/Israel to plunder and trample them like mud in the streets.

f.g: Here, a godless or profane nation.

n: But Assyria doesn’t see itself as God’s tool. Its goal is simply to destroy and conquer many nations.
Assyria’s king boasts: “Aren’t my commanders all kings?” His vassals are greater than other nations’ rulers.
He lists cities he conquered: Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, Damascus. Each fell like the others — so why would Jerusalem be different?

f.g: A major city on the Euphrates, taken by Assyria in 717 BC.

n: He has conquered kingdoms whose idols were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria.
Since he destroyed Samaria and its idols, why not Jerusalem? He wrongly counts the Lord as just another idol.
When God has finished His disciplinary work on Zion and Jerusalem, He will punish the Assyrian king’s arrogant heart and proud looks.

f.w: the stout heart of the king of Assyria

n: The king brags that he did it all by his own strength and wisdom: moving borders, seizing treasures, and toppling rulers.

f.w: By the strength of my hand

n: He boasts he gathered nations’ wealth like eggs from an unguarded nest — no one flapped a wing or chirped.
Can an axe boast against the one who swings it? Assyria is only a tool in God’s hand, yet acts as though it were the one in charge.
So God will send wasting disease among Assyria’s strong warriors and a fire beneath its glory.

f.g: Wasting sickness among the sturdy warriors.

n: Israel’s Light — the Holy One — will become a fire that burns up Assyria’s thorns and briers in one day.

f.w: the light of Israel shall be for a fire

n: It will consume the glory of Assyria’s forest and fields, body and soul — they will waste away like a sick man (or a fainting standard-bearer).

f.g: Possibly “as when a sick man wastes away.”

n: So few trees will remain that a child could count them — Assyria’s army will be decimated.

f.w: that a child may write them
f.g: So few a child could list them.

n: In that day, Israel’s remnant will no longer lean on the nation that struck them (as Ahaz leaned on Assyria) but will rely truly on the Holy One of Israel.
“A remnant shall return” — the meaning of the name of Isaiah’s son Shearjashub — to the Mighty God.
Though Israel be as numerous as sand, only a remnant will return. The destruction decreed will overflow with righteousness — justice that leads to a purified people.

f.w: a remnant of them shall return

n: The Lord will carry out the decreed destruction throughout the land.
God comforts His people in Zion: don’t fear Assyria, even though it strikes you as Egypt once did.

f.w: be not afraid of the Assyrian

n: In a very short time God’s anger against Judah will end and turn to Assyria’s destruction.
God will lash Assyria as He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb in Gideon’s day, and lift His rod as He did over the Red Sea against Egypt.

f.w: as his rod was upon the sea

n: Assyria’s burden and yoke will be lifted from Judah’s neck and broken “because of the anointing” — through God’s anointed one. Many see a pointer to the Messiah, the Anointed.

f.g: Possibly “because of fatness” in Hebrew; often read as pointing to the Anointed One.

n: Isaiah pictures the Assyrian army marching toward Jerusalem from the north, town by town: Aiath, Migron, Michmash, where it stores its baggage.
They cross the pass and camp at Geba; Ramah trembles; Gibeah, Saul’s hometown, flees.
Gallim, Laish, and poor Anathoth (Jeremiah’s hometown) cry out in alarm.
Madmenah and Gebim evacuate in panic. Each town is a few miles closer to Jerusalem.
The army halts at Nob, within sight of Jerusalem, and shakes its fist at Mount Zion.

f.g: A town just north of Jerusalem, within view of the city.

n: Then God steps in: like a forester He lops off the branches with terrifying power, felling the tall and proud. Assyria’s army was devastated before Jerusalem in 701 BC.
He cuts down the forest thickets with iron, and Lebanon’s great trees — Assyria’s might — fall before the Mighty One. Chapter 11 then shows a new shoot growing from a stump.
